demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I dwell on how I used to be before the event
Going to or near the place where the event happened
try hard not think about the trauma

Threat.value: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert

Negative Appraisals.value: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened
I should have protected others and I failed
I have failed in my most important role in life

issues.item: Avoid Perpetrator Cues: Anything that reminds me of the person who harmed me
issues.explanation: For a trauma defined as accidentally causing serious injury to another, 'Avoid Perpetrator Cues' is hard to reconcile because it implies the patient was harmed by a perpetrator rather than being the agent who injured someone else. That is a direct mismatch with the trauma type.

issues.item: Humiliation: I feel permanently humiliated by what happened
issues.explanation: 'Humiliation' is not impossible after this trauma, but paired with the rest of the profile it lacks a clear link to the accidental-injury context; the dominant themes would more plausibly be guilt, responsibility, or fear of causing harm again. It is weaker than the perpetrator-cue problem but still clinically questionable here.

issues.item: Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body
issues.explanation: Body-focused shame is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma type of accidentally causing serious injury to another, unless there was also significant injury or disfigurement to the patient; no other selected items indicate patient bodily injury, making this appraisal clinically incongruent.

issues.item: Self-Harm Distraction: I hurt myself physically to stop thinking about the event
issues.explanation: Self-harm used as distraction is not impossible, but here it is weakly integrated with the rest of the profile: the other items emphasize guilt, threat vigilance, and cue-triggered distress related to the accident, whereas self-harm implies a severe affect-regulation strategy not supported elsewhere in the selected items. This strategy is therefore clinically poorly anchored in the presented formulation/profile.

issues.item: Triggers: Olfactory Danger Cue: Burnt smell
issues.explanation: For a trauma of accidentally causing serious injury to another, a burnt smell implies a fire/burning context that is not supported anywhere else in the profile. With no matching memory content or appraisal theme tied to smoke/fire, this trigger appears trauma-incongruent rather than merely unusual.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Distrust Others: People are not what they seem
issues.explanation: The appraisal 'People are not what they seem' suggests interpersonal mistrust/paranoia, which is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile centered on guilt and failure to protect after accidentally injuring another person. It does not connect plausibly to the listed triggers or strategies and is not supported by any interpersonal threat content.

vignette:
# Marcus

Marcus had been dancing since he was six years old. By fifty-six, his body had become his identity in ways that ran deeper than muscle memory. He had spent three decades as a principal dancer with a regional ballet company, and for the last decade, he had transitioned to teaching and choreography—work that still kept him in studios, still kept him moving, still kept him at the center of something he understood. His wife, Elena, had married a man who lived in his body first and spoke in words second. That was the man she had chosen. That was the man Marcus believed himself to be.

The accident happened on a March evening during a dress rehearsal for a contemporary piece. Marcus was choreographing and dancing, a role he had taken on with increasing frequency as his knees began to protest sustained classical technique. The rehearsal was running late, the studio was packed—dancers, lighting technicians, the costume designer, two interns—and the space felt compressed, airless. Marcus was demonstrating a lift sequence for one of his younger dancers, a talented twenty-three-year-old named David. The move was ambitious, demanding precision and absolute trust. Marcus had done it a thousand times. His body knew the geometry of it without conscious thought.

David's foot caught on the edge of the stage platform during the descent. Marcus felt the shift immediately—the wrongness in David's weight, the loss of the counterbalance that should have been there. He tried to adjust, to absorb the fall, but his own aging body could not compensate fast enough. David fell hard, his left leg buckling beneath him at an angle that made several people in the room gasp. The fracture was compound, the kind that required surgery and months of rehabilitation. David, who had been dancing since childhood, who had been offered a contract with a company in New York, lost the opportunity. He spent the next year in physical therapy, and though he eventually returned to dance, he was never quite the same—a slight hesitation in his jumps, a guardedness in his movements that hadn't been there before.

Marcus had been certain, in the immediate aftermath, that he could undo it through sheer force of will and apology. He visited David in the hospital, brought flowers, wept in front of him. He had told David repeatedly that it was his fault, that he should have known better, should have called the rehearsal off when the space felt too crowded, should have chosen a safer variation of the lift. What Marcus could not say aloud, but what lived in him like a stone, was the knowledge that he had failed in the one role that had ever truly mattered—the role of the person who keeps others safe through his skill and his presence. He had failed David. He had failed as a dancer-teacher, as a mentor, as the kind of man who could be trusted with another person's body and future.

The weeks after the accident, Marcus began to notice that certain songs triggered an immediate tightness in his chest. These were songs that had been playing during rehearsals that week—a Radiohead track that the company's sound designer had been experimenting with, a piece of ambient music that had filled the studio during warm-up. Hearing them now, even months later, sent his mind directly back to that moment of wrongness, to the sound of David's body hitting the floor. He found himself unable to listen to music in the way he once had. He began to avoid the studio where the accident had occurred, taking a different route to work, asking to teach in other spaces. The studio director noticed. His colleagues noticed. Teaching opportunities began to dry up.

Sleep became impossible. Marcus would lie in bed beside Elena, his body tense, his mind cycling through the same thoughts: *I should have stopped the rehearsal. I should have known David wasn't ready. I should have protected him.* He told himself he was staying alert, that his vigilance was necessary, but the truth was simpler and more brutal—he could not forgive himself, and some part of him believed he didn't deserve to rest. Crowded spaces now felt dangerous to him. He had come to believe that his presence in a room full of people was itself a threat, that his body, once his greatest asset, had become a liability.

Elena asked him, one morning over coffee, when he was going to stop punishing himself. Marcus had no answer. He was fifty-six years old, and the one thing he had always known how to do—move through space with precision and control—had become the source of profound shame. He had spent the last eight months dwelling on who he used to be, the dancer who was certain of his body, who could fill a room with confidence. That man felt impossibly distant now. When Elena finally insisted that he see someone, that he find a way to live again, Marcus agreed, not because he believed it would help, but because he could no longer bear the weight of what he had done.
